summary: Defines how OSPF advertises link attributes on a per-application basis, so applications such as RSVP-TE, Segment Routing Policy and Loop-Free Alternates need not share one set of values. It is standards-track and was replaced by RFC 9492.

eli5.summary: Different routing jobs may want different notes about the same link. This document lets each job have its own notes in OSPF messages. It was replaced by RFC 9492.

subtitle: Application-specific link attributes for OSPF routing.

tldr.problem: Multiple applications (RSVP-TE, Segment Routing Policy, Loop-Free Alternates) use OSPF link attributes for traffic engineering, but there is no way to indicate which application uses which value, or to advertise different values for the same attribute per application.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8920 defines a new Application-Specific Link Attributes (ASLA) sub-TLV for OSPFv2 and OSPFv3. The sub-TLV includes an application identifier bit mask to tag which application(s) should use the advertised values, allowing different applications to have different settings on the same link.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can mix RSVP-TE, SR Policy, and LFA in the same OSPF network without confusion about which values apply to which application, and each application can have its own optimized attribute values. RFC 9492 later updated this specification.

today: RFC 8920 is a Proposed Standard. It was obsoleted by RFC 9492, which added refinements based on operational experience.

sections.title: The Problem of Multiple Applications
sections.content:
The Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) protocol is used in routers to advertise information about network links for routing decisions. For traffic engineering, routers advertise properties of each link: its bandwidth, delay, loss rates, administrative groups (colors), and other metrics. These properties help routing software compute paths that meet specific requirements.

Historically, these link properties were used by RSVP-TE, the Resource Reservation Protocol for traffic engineering. But other applications now need the same information. Segment Routing Policy uses these attributes to compute explicit paths based on constraints. Loop-Free Alternates use them to choose fast backup routes. The problem is that OSPF has no built-in way to say which application needs each advertised value. If RSVP-TE routers and SR Policy routers mix in the same network, an old RSVP-TE router might wrongly interpret an SR Policy advertisement as evidence that RSVP-TE is enabled on a link, causing path setup failures. Worse, different applications may need different values for the same attribute on the same link.
sections.eli5: If you ask a router for directions and it says "the road is narrow", it might mean the road is too narrow for trucks but fine for cars. Different routing protocols care about different details. OSPF needed a way to say which detail is for which routing protocol.

sections.title: Legacy Advertisements and Extended Link TLVs
sections.content:
OSPF has two main advertisement mechanisms for link attributes. The first is the TE Opaque LSA in OSPFv2 and the Intra-Area-TE-LSA in OSPFv3 (defined in RFC 3630 and RFC 5329). These carry attributes like administrative group, bandwidth, and metrics. They were designed for RSVP-TE and include no way to mark which application should use them.

The second mechanism is the Extended Link Opaque LSA in OSPFv2 (RFC 7684) and the E-Router-LSA in OSPFv3 (RFC 8362). These were introduced as generic containers to advertise link attributes for applications other than RSVP-TE or GMPLS. The advantage of these extended LSAs is that they clearly separate non-RSVP-TE attributes from the legacy TE advertisements, avoiding confusion about which application each value is for.

RFC 8920 builds on the Extended Link TLV approach. It keeps all legacy advertisements unchanged but adds a new Application-Specific Link Attributes (ASLA) sub-TLV within the Extended Link TLV structure. This sub-TLV carries an application identifier bit mask plus the attribute values themselves, letting each application have its own values.
sections.eli5: OSPF can advertise link attributes in two old ways (one for RSVP-TE, one for others) with no labels. RFC 8920 adds a new sub-container inside the "others" section that lets you label which app each value is for.

sections.title: The Application-Specific Link Attributes Sub-TLV
sections.content:
The ASLA sub-TLV has Type 10 in OSPFv2 and Type 11 in OSPFv3. It lives inside the Extended Link TLV in OSPFv2 or the Router-Link TLV in OSPFv3. The structure is straightforward: it begins with a Standard Application Identifier Bit Mask (SABM) Length field and a User-Defined Application Identifier Bit Mask (UDABM) Length field, each limited to 0, 4, or 8 octets.

The Standard Application Identifier Bit Mask has three defined bits: bit 0 for RSVP-TE, bit 1 for Segment Routing Policy, and bit 2 for Loop-Free Alternates. These bits are shared with RFC 8919 (the IS-IS equivalent) to maintain consistency across routing protocols.

The User-Defined Application Identifier Bit Mask supports proprietary or experimental applications. Following the bit masks come the actual link attribute values, encoded in the same format as legacy RSVP-TE advertisements. By reusing the legacy format, the ASLA sub-TLV can carry any link attribute: SRLG, bandwidth, delay, loss, administrative group, and others.

Multiple ASLA sub-TLVs can appear in the same Extended Link TLV if different applications need different attributes or different values for the same attribute. A router chooses the first matching advertisement when multiple values are advertised for the same application and attribute.
sections.eli5: Each ASLA sub-TLV is a labeled container. The label lists which apps should use the attributes inside (using bit flags). The attributes are written in the same old format, just now with a label saying who they are for.

sections.title: Deployment and Migration
sections.content:
RFC 8920 is designed for gradual deployment. Networks with old routers and new routers can interoperate during migration.

Scenario 1 (legacy coexistence): If RSVP-TE needs legacy advertisements but SR Policy or LFA can use ASLA sub-TLVs, routers advertise RSVP-TE attributes in the old TE Opaque LSA or Intra-Area-TE-LSA, and SR Policy/LFA attributes in the Extended Link TLV with ASLA sub-TLVs. Old OSPF routers see the legacy advertisements and process them; new routers see both and use the right one for each application.

Scenario 2 (all attributes shared): If all applications use the same values on a link, the network can use legacy advertisements only. This avoids duplication and works with old routers.

Migration from legacy: To migrate a network from legacy advertisements to ASLA sub-TLVs: (1) upgrade all routers; (2) send both legacy and ASLA advertisements (duplication); (3) enable ASLA processing on all routers; (4) remove legacy advertisements when ready.

RFC 8920 notes that RSVP-TE attributes SHOULD continue using legacy advertisements for backward compatibility rather than switching to ASLA sub-TLVs. New attributes defined in future RFCs MUST support application-specific values via ASLA sub-TLVs, with no legacy fallback.
sections.eli5: Old routers and new routers can work together during the switch. The network can gradually add labels to link properties without breaking anything.

sections.title: Security and Impact
sections.content:
OSPF normally operates within a single administrative domain, but implementations may run in networks where potential attackers have access to parts of the domain. OSPF supports strong authentication via HMAC-SHA (RFC 5709), IPsec (RFC 4552), and other mechanisms. All of these protections apply to the ASLA sub-TLVs defined in RFC 8920.

Routers must handle malformed ASLA sub-TLVs gracefully. If a router receives a sub-TLV with an invalid length field, it should drop the sub-TLV and log the event. To prevent denial-of-service attacks from malformed TLVs, logging should be rate-limited.

RFC 8920 itself does not introduce new security risks because it only adds labels to existing link attribute advertisements. If an attacker tampers with an ASLA sub-TLV labeled for SR Policy, the impact is limited to SR Policy path computation; RSVP-TE is unaffected. The same authentication mechanisms that protect legacy IS-IS or OSPF advertisements also protect the new application-specific ones.
sections.eli5: The security is the same as before. Routers check that messages are not forged. Now they also know which app each message is for, so tampering with one app does not affect others.
